## The library everyone imports, nobody opens {background-color="#0b1021"}

Pandas, PyTorch, scikit-learn, JAX, every dataframe and ML stack…

. . .

They all bottom out in **NumPy**.

. . .

So let's look at something completely ordinary:

```{pyodide}
import numpy as np
a = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40])
a // 3          # integer floor division on an array
```

. . .

What actually happens under this? It's weirder - and faster - than you'd think.

# Part 1 — Why is `a // b` slow? {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

## Division is the slow arithmetic {.smaller}

Not all CPU instructions cost the same. Rough latencies on a modern x86 core:

| Operation | Approx. latency (cycles) |
|-----------|--------------------------:|
| add / sub | ~1 |
| multiply  | ~3 |
| **integer divide** | **~20–90** |

. . .

Multiply is cheap. **Divide is the expensive one nobody thinks about.**

. . .

And in NumPy you rarely divide *once* — you divide across a whole array,
millions of times. That cost is multiplied.

::: {.notes}
Exact numbers vary by microarchitecture; the point is the order-of-magnitude
gap between divide and everything else.
:::

## The key idea

> You can replace **division by a constant** with a **multiply and a shift**.

. . .

Dividing by 7? A compiler doesn't emit a `div`. It multiplies by a cleverly
chosen "magic number" and shifts:

```c
// x / 7  becomes roughly:
q = (x * 0x2492_4925ULL) >> 34;   // magic constant + shift
```

. . .

This is the trick behind **`libdivide`** - and the foundation of everything
that follows.

# Part 2 — The multiply-and-shift trick {background-color="#16213e"}

## Bringing libdivide into NumPy {.smaller}

The catch: in an array op like `a // b`, the divisor `b` is often the **same
value repeated**. Compute the magic number **once**, reuse it across the array.

```c
// Precompute once per divisor
struct libdivide_s64_t d = libdivide_s64_gen(divisor);

// Then, for every element — no hardware divide!
for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    out[i] = libdivide_s64_do(a[i], &d);
}
```

. . .

**PR #17727** - added libdivide to floor division. First real speedup.

. . .

We also had to get **floor** semantics right: Python's `//` rounds toward
**negative infinity**, C's `/` truncates toward **zero**.

```{pyodide}
import numpy as np
# NumPy matches Python's floor semantics, not C's truncation:
np.array([-7]) // 2, -7 // 2, int(-7 / 2)   # -4, -4, -3
```

::: {.notes}
This floor-vs-truncate detail is exactly the kind of thing that bites you
later. Foreshadow the bug. Run the cell live so the -4 vs -3 lands.
:::

# Part 3 — Going SIMD, portably {background-color="#0f3460"}

## One divide at a time is still one at a time {.smaller}

libdivide removed the hardware `div`. But we still process **one element per
loop iteration**.

. . .

**SIMD** — Single Instruction, Multiple Data — does 4, 8, 16 elements *at once*:

```text
scalar:   [a0] / d  →  [a1] / d  →  [a2] / d  →  [a3] / d
SIMD:     [a0 a1 a2 a3] / d   →   all four, one instruction
```

. . .

But which instruction? AVX2? AVX-512? ARM NEON? They're all different.

## Universal intrinsics: write once, run fast everywhere {.smaller}

NumPy has its own SIMD abstraction layer. You write **one** loop against
generic intrinsics; NumPy compiles specialized versions per architecture and
picks the best one **at runtime**.

```c
// One source, ~generic intrinsics
npyv_s32 a = npyv_load_s32(src);
npyv_s32 q = npyv_divc_s32(a, divisor);   // vectorized divide-by-constant
npyv_store_s32(dst, q);
```

. . .

- **PR #18075** — SIMD dispatch for **unsigned** floor division
- **PR #18766** — **signed** integer division via universal intrinsics

. . .

Signed is the hard one: sign handling + floor rounding, all vectorized.

## Which instruction runs *here*? {.smaller}

NumPy will tell you, **per ufunc and per dtype**, which SIMD variant it built
and which it picked at runtime — let's ask about `floor_divide` itself:

```{pyodide}
import numpy as np
# 'l' = the int64 loop ('lll' = int64 // int64 -> int64)
np.lib.introspect.opt_func_info(func_name="floor_divide", signature="l")
```

::: {.callout-note}
Live here it runs in a **WASM sandbox** (Pyodide), so it reports the browser's
build. On my laptop (Apple Silicon) the same call returns:
:::

```python
{'floor_divide': {'lll': {'available': 'baseline(NEON NEON_FP16 ... ASIMD)',
                          'current':   'baseline(NEON NEON_FP16 ... ASIMD)'}}}
# On an x86 box you'd instead see 'available': 'SSE41 ... AVX2 AVX512...'
# and 'current' set to whichever your CPU supports.
```

::: {.notes}
opt_func_info is the money slide: it names the exact ufunc + type-code loop the
whole talk is about. Drop the signature filter to show every int dtype
(bbb, hhh, iii, lll, qqq + unsigned). If you can, run it from a REAL terminal on
the laptop live. Related: np.show_runtime() (my PR #21468) gives the CPU-level view.
:::

# Part 4 — The bug I shipped 😬 {background-color="#3a0ca3"}

## A ufunc is a *table*, tried in order {.smaller}

`floor_divide` isn't one function — it's an **ordered list of typed loops**,
one per dtype. When you write `a // b`, NumPy scans this list **top-to-bottom**
and runs the **first loop your inputs fit into**:

```{pyodide}
import numpy as np
np.floor_divide.types   # 'in in -> out' — note bb->b (signed) before BB->B (unsigned)
```

. . .

The rule: for each width, the **signed** loop must be listed **before** the
**unsigned** one (`bb->b` before `BB->B`, `ll->l` before `LL->L`, …).

. . .

My SIMD change **(#18075)** accidentally emitted the **unsigned loops first**.

## Fast code that's wrong isn't fast {.smaller}

With unsigned listed first, some inputs matched an **unsigned** loop when they
should have hit the **signed** one — and reinterpreting signed bits as unsigned
turns small negatives into huge positives:

```{pyodide}
import numpy as np
# This is *why* loop order matters — a signed value seen as unsigned:
np.array([-6], dtype=np.int64).view(np.uint64)   # 18446744073709551610
```

. . .

So `a // b` came back **silently wrong** for certain type combos — fast,
vectorized, SIMD-accelerated, and incorrect. Shipped to *millions*. 😬

. . .

Caught **downstream by pandas** (pandas#40874), *not* by our own tests.

> The part most performance talks skip: sometimes you're the one who broke it.

## The fix, and closing the gap {.smaller}

**PR #18751** — one-line reorder: put signed back before unsigned in
`generate_umath.py`.

. . .

The real fix was the **test**: assert signed-before-unsigned for *every* ufunc,
so this class of bug can never silently return.

. . .

A separate edge-case saga from the same area — `INT_MIN // -1` **overflows**
(the true answer doesn't fit in the type). What should NumPy do? → **#21507,
#21727** report it gracefully instead of silent UB:

```{pyodide}
import numpy as np
imin = np.iinfo(np.int64).min          # -9223372036854775808
np.array([imin], dtype=np.int64) // np.int64(-1)   # warns: overflow
```

::: {.notes}
Loop table: `np.floor_divide.types`. Casting rules mean the resolver can land on
the wrong loop if unsigned precedes signed. The .view() cell shows the hazard of
signed->unsigned reinterpretation (illustrative, not the literal buggy output).
INT_MIN/-1: abs(INT_MIN) doesn't fit in the type — the classic overflow.
:::

# Part 5 — What I'd want you to take away {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

## Takeaways {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
1. **Division is expensive** — and multiply-and-shift is a beautiful way to
   dodge it
2. **SIMD portability is real** — universal intrinsics let one codebase go
   fast on Intel, AMD, and ARM
3. **Real OSS performance work** = benchmarks + review + mistakes + recovery,
   not just clever code
4. The code under your `import` is **approachable**. You can contribute to it.
:::
